claims.text: The powder feedstock is a cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi high-entropy alloy.
Gas atomization produces the AlCrFeNiSi powder with a homogeneous initial composition.
Build-plate preheating during additive manufacturing reduces thermal gradients in AlCrFeNiSi.
Reduced thermal gradients lower residual stresses in additively manufactured AlCrFeNiSi.
Build-plate preheating minimizes compositional segregation in additively manufactured AlCrFeNiSi.
Build-plate preheating decreases defect formation in additively manufactured AlCrFeNiSi.
Lower residual stress, segregation, and defect formation improve the mechanical integrity of fabricated AlCrFeNiSi.
The proposed build-plate preheating range is approximately 400–600 °C.
Laser energy density and powder-feedstock characteristics are held constant when comparing preheated and non-preheated builds.
Reduced thermal gradients produce a more uniform microstructure and more consistent grain growth.
Reduced thermal gradients decrease segregation at grain boundaries.
Preheating locally slows the cooling rate during additive manufacturing.
Rapid temperature gradients cause heterogeneous phase formation and defect generation.
Preheated AlCrFeNiSi builds will have higher tensile strength than otherwise identical non-preheated builds.
Preheated AlCrFeNiSi builds will have greater ductility than otherwise identical non-preheated builds.
The benefit and optimal temperature of preheating may vary across alloys and additive-manufacturing methods.
The proposed experiment compares a non-preheated control with a build preheated to approximately 500 °C while holding laser power and scan speed constant.
The hypothesis is falsified if preheating fails to produce statistically significant reductions in residual stress, segregation, and defect density together with improved mechanical properties.
